claims.text: Order: roots → trunks → divisions → cords → terminal nerves, running from the neck to the proximal upper limb.
claims.quote: The brachial plexus consists of roots, trunks, divisions, cords, and terminal nerves; it ranges from the neck to the proximal upper limb.

claims.text: Roots: the ventral rami of C5–C8 and T1; every root of the plexus carries both sensory and motor fibers.
claims.quote: The five roots of the brachial plexus emerge from the vertebral column. They consist of the ventral rami of spinal nerves C5-C8 and T1. It is important not to confuse the roots of the brachial plexus with the dorsal (sensory) and ventral (motor) roots of a spinal nerve. All of the roots of the brachial plexus contain both sensory and motor fibers.

claims.text: Branches from the roots: dorsal scapular nerve (posterior C5 root) to the rhomboids and levator scapulae; long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7) to serratus anterior.
claims.quote: Dorsal scapular nerve: arises from the posterior aspect of the C5 root and supplies the rhomboid muscles and levator scapulae Long thoracic nerve: from C5,C6 and C7 to supply serratus anterior

claims.text: Trunks: form between scalenus anterior and medius: upper trunk = C5 + C6, middle trunk = C7, lower trunk = C8 + T1.
claims.quote: Trunks form from the roots as they pass between the scalenus anterior and medius muscles. C5 and C6 roots combine to form the upper or superior trunk, C7 root comprises the middle trunk, and C8 and T1 roots combine to form the lower or inferior trunk.

claims.text: Branches from the trunks: suprascapular nerve (upper trunk) to supraspinatus and infraspinatus, with sensation to the glenohumeral and acromioclavicular joints; nerve to subclavius (upper trunk).
claims.quote: suprascapular nerve: arises from the upper trunk and supplies the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles, and sensation to the glenohumeral and acromioclavicular joints; Nerve to subclavius: from the upper trunk, supplies the subclavius muscle

claims.text: Divisions: each trunk splits into an anterior and a posterior division behind the mid clavicle; anterior divisions supply the anterior (flexor) compartments, posterior divisions the posterior (extensor) compartments; no branches arise from the divisions.
claims.quote: Each trunk divides to form an anterior and posterior division posterior to the mid clavicle. In general, anterior division nerves supply muscles of the anterior compartments of the upper limb (flexors), whereas the posterior division nerves supply muscles of the posterior compartments (extensors). No branches arise directly from the divisions.

claims.text: Cords: named for their relation to the second part of the axillary artery: lateral cord = anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks; medial cord = anterior division of the lower trunk; posterior cord = all three posterior divisions.
claims.quote: The divisions combine to form cords, which are named for their relationship to the second part of the axillary artery: lateral cord is formed by the union of the anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks at the lateral border of the first rib medial cord is a continuation of the anterior division of the lower trunk posterior cord consists of the union of the three posterior divisions

claims.text: Lateral cord branches: lateral pectoral nerve (C5, 6, 7), musculocutaneous nerve (C5, 6, 7) and the lateral root of the median nerve.
claims.quote: Branches from the lateral cord are: lateral pectoral nerve: C5, 6, 7 musculocutaneous nerve: C5, 6, 7 lateral root of the median nerve: C5, 6, 7, (C8, T1)

claims.text: Posterior cord branches: upper and lower subscapular nerves (C5, 6), thoracodorsal nerve (C6, 7, 8), radial nerve (C5–T1) and axillary nerve (C5, 6).
claims.quote: Branches from the posterior cord are: upper subscapular nerve: C5, 6 thoracodorsal nerve: C6, 7, 8 lower subscapular nerve: C5, 6 radial nerve: C5, 6, 7, 8, T1 axillary nerve: C5, 6

claims.text: Medial cord branches: medial pectoral nerve and medial cutaneous nerves of the arm and forearm (all C8, T1), the medial root of the median nerve, and the ulnar nerve ((C7), C8, T1).
claims.quote: Branches from the medial cord are: medial pectoral nerve: C8, T1 medial cutaneous nerve of the arm: C8, T1 medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm: C8, T1 medial root of the median nerve: (C5, 6, 7), C8, T1 ulnar nerve: (C7), C8, T1

claims.text: Long thoracic nerve course: descends behind the roots of the plexus, then runs a long course down the chest wall in the mid-axillary line on the surface of serratus anterior, which it supplies.
claims.quote: The nerve descends posterior to the roots of the brachial plexus and anterior to the scalenus posterior muscle and has a long course along the chest wall in the mid-axillary line to lie on the superficial surface of the serratus anterior muscle, which it innervates.

claims.text: Long thoracic nerve injury: its long, superficial course leaves it open to direct trauma or stretch (backpack palsy) and to surgery such as mastectomy with axillary node clearance; the palsy causes scapular winging because serratus anterior no longer holds the scapula against the chest wall.
claims.quote: The long thoracic nerve is susceptible to damage (causing backpack palsy) due to its long and superficial course either from direct trauma or stretching of the nerve. Damage to the nerve may also occur during surgical procedures including thoracoplasty, axillary nodal clearance, mastectomy and resection of the first rib. The risk of injury to the long thoracic nerve is far greater in patients following a radical mastectomy (with clearance of the axillary lymph nodes) compared with simple mastectomy. Long thoracic nerve palsy causes winging of the scapula as the serratus anterior muscle no longer holds the scapula against the chest wall.

claims.text: Plexus lesion pattern: limb pain with motor or sensory deficits that do not match a single nerve root or peripheral nerve distribution.
claims.quote: Manifestations of plexus disorders include extremity pain and motor or sensory deficits that do not correspond to an isolated nerve root or peripheral nerve distribution.
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Plexus Disorders

claims.text: Acute brachial neuritis: severe supraclavicular pain, then weakness and diminished reflexes as the pain resolves; serratus anterior (scapular winging), other upper-trunk muscles and anterior interosseous muscles are most often affected.
claims.quote: In acute brachial neuritis, findings include severe supraclavicular pain, weakness, and diminished reflexes, with minor sensory abnormalities in the distribution of the brachial plexus. Usually, weakness develops and reflexes decrease as pain resolves. Severe weakness develops within 3 to 10 days, then typically regresses over the next few months. The most commonly affected muscles are the serratus anterior (causing winging of the scapula), other muscles innervated by the upper trunk, and muscles innervated by the anterior interosseous nerve in the forearm—patients may not be able to make an ο with the thumb and index finger.
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Plexus Disorders

claims.text: Lower plexus (C8 to T1): injury mainly affects the forearm and hand muscles.
claims.quote: Lower plexus (C8 to T1): Primarily affects muscles of the forearm and hand

claims.text: Klumpke palsy: a rare lower plexus injury: hand and wrist weakness or paralysis, absent grasp reflex with the biceps reflex present, often an ipsilateral Horner syndrome from T1 sympathetic fibers.
claims.quote: Klumpke palsy is rare and is a lower plexus injury that causes weakness or paralysis of the hand and wrist. The grasp reflex is usually absent, but the biceps reflex is present. Often, the sympathetic fibers of T1 are involved causing an ipsilateral Horner syndrome (miosis, ptosis, facial anhidrosis).
